text.p: These are significant stories in the Nigerian press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Nigeria's government is to ban the importation of bitumen on the advice of the National Economic Intelligence Committee. Money that would have been spent importing bitumen will instead be spent developing local sources of the material.
- A total of 52 out of Nigeria's 115 banks are in a condition of distress, a report from the central bank says.
- State-run National Fertiliser Company says its production is limited by inadequate funding.

- Collection of tolls from users of bridges in the commercial capital, Lagos, may begin before the end of 1997. Sources at the works' ministry say details of the scheme are to be worked out by August.
- Afribank has concluded plans to launch an advertising campaign estimated to cost over 30 million naira.
- Prospects of an end to petrol shortages rise with the first deliveries of imported fuel to filling stations in and around Lagos at the weekend.
- Royal Dutch Shell's Nigerian producing unit has drawn up plans for a resumption of activities in southeastern Ogoniland, after being driven out by sabotage in 1993.

- Nigeria loses 26 billion naira annually to illegal importation of palm oil, refined vegetable oil and tallow, the managing director of Okitipupa Oil Palm Plc says. He said 900,000 tonnes of palm oil were being produced annually, while 720,000 tonnes are imported.

- The government may in principle have approved the dedication of 100,000 bpd of crude oil to finance ongoing projects by the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation, and to pay for the 120 million litres of petroleum products being imported to end the current fuel shortage. The 100,000 bpd would be removed from the current allocation to refineries of 250,000 bpd.
- Government has ordered the Kaduna-based Federal Superphosphate Fertiliser Company to produce 14,000 tonnes of fertiliser this year, to end a national scarcity.
- Some filling stations in the Lagos area are selling fuel at between 20 and 25 naira per litre, ignoring the government's fixed price of 11 naira per litre.
